newsitem.title: GREECE: OLYMPICS-ELATED ATHENS ROLLS UP SLEEVES TO WIN 2004 GAMES.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-ELATED ATHENS ROLLS UP SLEEVES TO WIN 2004 GAMES.

text.p: Elated over being shortlisted to host the 2004 summer Olympics, Athens vowed to work on its shortcomings and bring the world's biggest sports festival back to its birthplace.

"It was a great success for the Greek effort," Greek Deputy Foreign Minister George Papandreou told reporters. "From now on we will make a more systematic effort to be the final choice on September 5."

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) selected on Friday Athens, Buenos Aires, Cape Town, Rome and Stockholm as the final candidates from among 11 cities bidding to host the 2004 Summer Games. It will make its final decision in September.

"In the next six months we will repay the confidence they showed in Athens by strengthening our bid and assuring all IOC members that Athens desires, is able and has the capacity to host the 2004 Games," Athens bidding committee president Yanna Angelopoulos said in a statement.
A sprawling city of four million people, Athens was so incensed at losing the centennial 1996 Games to Atlanta that it vowed never to bid again.
But it changed its mind and decided to go for the 2004 Games on merit and not as a sentimental favourite because the ancient Olympics originated in Greece and they were revived in Athens in 1896.
Athens has projected a modern image of a city with top facilities, such as an 80,000-seat Olympic Stadium and two indoor stadiums.
It is working on a $2.1 billion subway system and a new $2.5 billion international airport, and plans to build an Olympic village, roads and other sports facilities to cope with demand.

"Effort should now be focused on our weaknesses, which are traffic, the environment and hotels," Athens bidding committee member Lucas Papademos, who is also governor of Greece's central bank, told reporters.
The IOC has praised the Athens bid for enjoying widespread public support but pointed out there were finacial, transport and environmental concerns.
Environmentalists have slammed the bid file, saying it spelled disaster for an overdeveloped city already burdened with heavy smog.

"The existing planning will worsen the problems identified by the IOC instead of resolving them. It needs radical changes to help the city cope with chronic environmental problems," said Nikos Charalambidis, a spokesman for the Greek office of the international Greenpeace organisation.

A budding local movement, which predicts the Games would be an environmental, city planning and financial disaster for Athens, said it hoped the IOC would be less impressed by the bid when it examined it closer in the next few months.
"The bid will come under more scrutiny in the next stage," said architect Panayotis Dotsikas, a spokesman for the Citizens Initiative Against Hosting the 2004 Olympics in Athens.
"There will be time for any sensible person to understand it is impossible to hold the 2004 Olympics in Athens," he added.
